title: Two faces of every action
goal: Recognize Polish verb pairs — one for an action in progress, one for an action completed — and choose between them.
bekal: recognizing the prefixes that mark a completed action
understanding why the completed form has no present tense

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Napisałeś już podanie?
dialogs.intro: A study desk in the library. The same assignment is still hanging over both of them.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: Have you finished the application yet?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pisałem wczoraj dwie godziny, ale nie skończyłem.
lines.id: I wrote for two hours yesterday, but I didn't finish.
lines.literal: I-wrote-ongoing yesterday two hours, but not I-finished-completed.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: So you were writing, but you didn't get it written.

lines.text: Ja też. Wczoraj czytałam artykuł trzy razy, zanim przeczytałam do końca.
lines.id: Me too. Yesterday I read the article three times before I finally got through it.
lines.literal: I too. yesterday I-read-ongoing article three times, before I-read-completed to end.

notes: **Almost every Polish verb lives in a pair.** One presents the action as an **activity** (*pisać* — write, be writing, usually write), the other presents it as a **finished result** (*napisać* — write something to completion).

**Pisałem, ale nie napisałem** is the key sentence of this unit. Literally "I was writing, but I didn't write it" — and in Polish that's not a strange sentence at all, but the most natural way to say "I worked on it but didn't finish".

**English handles this with extra words and tenses** — "was writing", "have written", "finished", "got done". Polish handles it by **choosing a different verb**. The meaning is the same; once again the marker has moved inside the word.

**Kupię ci jeden** — note that this is **not** the present tense. The completed form (*kupić*) has no present tense at all: give it present-tense endings and it automatically means the **future**. A surprising piece of good news — you can already talk about the future without learning any new forms.
**Zanim** means "before" and links two events: *Czytałam trzy razy, zanim przeczytałam do końca.*
**Zróbmy, skończmy** — the "let's" form almost always uses the **completed** verb, because you're inviting people to get something done, not to wallow in it.

**Jeszcze nie** — "not yet". Its partner: *już* (already). These two little words work together with the verb pairs: *Już napisałem* (I've finished writing it) vs *Jeszcze nie napisałem* (I haven't finished it yet).
**Na urodziny** — "for your birthday". Birthday in Polish is always plural (*urodziny*), like "births". The greeting: *Wszystkiego najlepszego!* (all the best).

grammars.title: Two faces, three tenses
body: Why this rule matters: your choice of form decides the **tense** of your sentence, not just its shade of meaning.
after: That empty "present" cell isn't a gap; it makes sense: something **completed** can't be in progress right now.

And since the completed form doesn't use its present-tense endings for anything else, they're recycled for the future. That's why *napiszę* means "I will write (it to the end)" — more on this in unit 19.
⚠️ When in doubt at A1, use the **ongoing** form. It's almost always understood, while a completed form in the wrong place can sound like an unfinished sentence.

grammars.title: How the pairs are formed
body: Three ways, and the first covers most of the verbs you know.
after: The prefix differs from verb to verb and **can't be guessed** — *zrobić* but *napisać*, *przeczytać* but *wypić*. So the only method that works: note down every new verb **as a pair**, from day one.
Look at the pair *kupować / kupić*: here it's the **shorter** form that's completed. The same goes for *dawać / dać*, *wracać / wrócić*, *zaczynać / zacząć*.

Some prefixes also change the **meaning**, not just the completeness: *pisać* (write) → *podpisać* (sign), *przepisać* (copy out), *zapisać* (write down, sign up). That's for A2; for now just know that one root can produce a whole family of words.

blocks.text: These twenty pairs cover almost every everyday A1 sentence. Learn them in pairs — drilling only one form is the most wasteful way to learn Polish.

blocks.title: Four sentences that show the difference
items: *Wczoraj czytałem książkę.* — Yesterday I was reading a book. (the activity)
*Wczoraj przeczytałem książkę.* — Yesterday I finished the book. (the result)
*Codziennie gotuję obiad.* — I cook lunch every day. (a habit → always ongoing)

blocks.text: The adverbs in the left column are **reliable clues**. If your sentence says "every day", the completed form is almost certainly wrong; if it says "finally", the ongoing form is almost certainly wrong.

blocks.title: Don't worry too much
items: This is the part of Polish that takes longest to sink in — foreigners who've lived in Poland for years still occasionally pick the wrong one.
Mistakes here **rarely get in the way of understanding**. What matters is the right verb; the right face can come later.
The most effective way to learn isn't memorizing rules but **collecting ready-made sentences**. Every time you hear a sentence that feels right, write it down whole.
